doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

chapter: Joan Rivers Show and Woody Herman
title: Touring with Woody Herman and the lucky break at Lincoln Center
summary: Herman's band got hotels and little money; a listener at a Beverly Sills party led to L.A. work, teaching Shear about networking.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: I assume when you were with Woody Herman maybe the road travel had improved some? Or was it still —

Well they treated us a little better on Woody Herman’s band than the other bands like Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey, which were known as ghost bands because the leader had died. But they had to sleep on the bus a lot, where Woody’s band never, we never had to sleep on the bus. There would always be a hotel. You wouldn’t make a lot of money at all. I hardly saved any money in those two years. So you know going in that you’re not going to make a lot of money, you’d better do it for the love of it and opportunities that might arise later on. And three months before I got off the band I played the retirement party for Beverly Sills, the opera singer, on the side of Lincoln Center they put up this giant tent with chefs and everything. And there was a guy that was listening to the band, because not too many people were listening, they were eating and chatting. And one guy and his wife were listening to the band and he came up to me and talked to me and we talked and he said when I got back to Los Angeles to give him a call. Turns out he was a very big composer of some big shows, and I fell into the scene right away because of that. Yeah, I just got lucky. So it’s networking. It’s one thing I didn’t get a lot of information from is networking, when I was in school. It was all about playing. It wasn’t about how to conduct yourself, although at that point you should know how to conduct yourself. But you have to know where to hang out and meet the right people and say the right things and have the right equipment, and all that stuff was not taught. You had to really — I learned that late and I should have learned it earlier.
